questions.q: How is an imported Apex method invoked imperatively?
options: By decorating it with @wire inside a method body
By calling it through this.template.querySelector
Exactly like any other JavaScript function that returns a Promise -- no decorator, no special syntax
Only from inside the constructor()
questions.explain: Once imported, an imperative call is just a normal Promise-returning function call -- there is no decorator or special syntax involved, unlike the wired approach.

questions.q: If an Apex method's signature is `getContactsBornAfter(Date birthDate)`, how is it called imperatively with a birthDate value?
options: getContactsBornAfter(birthDate)
@wire(getContactsBornAfter, birthDate)
getContactsBornAfter.call(birthDate)
getContactsBornAfter({ birthDate })
questions.explain: Parameters are passed as a single object whose keys exactly match the Apex method's parameter names, so `{ birthDate }` maps to the Apex parameter named birthDate.

questions.q: Which of the following is a scenario this lesson identifies as requiring an imperative call rather than @wire?
options: Loading a record's fields automatically as soon as the component renders
Re-running a query automatically whenever a reactive @api property changes
Any write/DML operation, since a method with side effects can never be marked cacheable=true
Displaying data that never changes after the component loads
questions.explain: Write operations (DML) can't be cacheable=true, which @wire requires -- so any write must go through an imperative call. The other scenarios listed are actually good fits for @wire, not reasons to avoid it.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say error handling 'matters more' for imperative calls than for wired calls?
options: A wired call's error lands visibly in the destructured error property almost unavoidably, while a rejected imperative call is easy to silently swallow if try/catch is forgotten, leaving the user with no feedback at all
Imperative calls never actually throw errors
Wired calls automatically retry on failure, so errors never need handling
Imperative calls run on a separate thread that ignores errors by default
questions.explain: A wired result's data/error shape makes an error hard to ignore once you're already looking at the destructured result. An imperative call's rejected Promise, by contrast, disappears silently without explicit try/catch or .catch() handling.

questions.q: What is the advantage of using async/await to chain several dependent imperative Apex calls, as in the createAccount/createContact example?
options: It makes the Apex calls run in parallel automatically
It is required syntax -- Apex calls cannot be chained any other way
It removes the need for any error handling at all
It lets the code read top-to-bottom like synchronous code, which is more readable than nesting multiple .then() callbacks for dependent calls
questions.explain: async/await lets dependent, sequential asynchronous calls read top-to-bottom, which is significantly more readable than nesting .then() callbacks for the same sequence of dependent operations.
